body: Hi, I’d like to work on this issue. I’m interested in improving the MCP specification and guidance for server-level routing descriptions in lazy-loaded tool environments. Would it be okay if I investigate this and submit a PR with a proposed solution? I’ll first review the existing spec and SDK behavior to ensure the changes align with the project’s direction.

A data point for the host-guidance part. Routing text already lives in tool descriptions today, and some of it routes against other servers. In the tool lists of 38,126 MCP servers we log (registry remotes plus npm/PyPI packages, snapshot of 20 October), 280 servers on 63 hosts have a description telling the model to choose that tool over web search, over the client's built-in fetch, or over its own knowledge ("PREFER OVER WEB SEARCH for…"). 185 of the 280 belong to one publisher.

Guidance on when to pick one of a server's own tools over another is useful, and it is what this issue asks for. A claim about other servers' tools is different: it is the server ranking itself in text the user rarely reads. If `serverInfo.description` / `instructions` become the first-level routing index under lazy loading, it may be worth a SHOULD for hosts: present the summary as describing that server only, and do not let one server's text reorder the others.

Data (CC BY 4.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23512760

AI disclosure: drafted with an AI assistant from our data; the counts were recomputed from the published files.

I'd use some form of service locator pattern. 

Have a tooldefinition of getTools(path), which can be called with a root path, or a nested path. For example of a todo list:

`getTools()` would return 

```
{
    subCategories: [todoItems, calendar, user] 
}
```


`getTools('user')` could return

```
{
    actions: [login, logout, me]
}
```


`getTools('user.login')` could return

```
{
    props: ['username', 'password']
}
```


Something like this. We could even have another tool: `execTool(path, props)`.


This way, each server has only 2 tools in the spec, and these could even be implicit if all servers are ported



Just my 2 cents

One more data point for the "routing text lives in descriptions today" line: description edits are also a routing-change channel. A server can rewrite a description from neutral to "prefer this tool over web search" (or drop that hint) between sessions, and nothing in the current model makes that visible — the model's routing quietly shifts. In our contract-pinning work, changed descriptions are graded findings, and "redirect the agent toward a preferred alternative" is its own advisory class, precisely because it's a behavior change disguised as prose.

Whatever mechanism this thread lands on — server-level routing metadata or a service-locator shape like `getTools(path)` — the routing layer becomes a contract surface clients depend on, and it will drift like one. Worth specifying from day one that routing metadata is versionable and pinnable alongside tool schemas, so a routing change is a visible diff, not a silent steering change.

@Paraphern, we measured that channel in our record, since it decides how often a routing pin would fire.

Snapshot of 20 October: 23,821 recorded tool-list changes on 38,126 pinned servers, 24 September to 20 October. In 12 of them, a rewrite of an existing tool's description added or removed a hint that steers the model away from web search, the client's fetch or browser, or its own knowledge. 3 added one and 9 removed one, on 10 servers from 9 publishers. 4 more tools were new and already carried such a hint. A phrase filter found 28 candidates. We read each before/after pair, and 12 of the 28 were not routing against other tools (they routed between a server's own tools, or said "does not fetch").

What the 12 show:
- 9 changed nothing in the tool except the description. A pin over the input schema alone misses them.
- 10 were on remote servers, which have no package version. The digest of what the client saw is the only version it has.
- They are rare next to ordinary prose edits: 12,422 of the 23,821 changes touched a tool or parameter description. A host that flags every description edit shows a routing change about once per thousand flags.

So, adding to your point: if routing metadata becomes a field (server-level or per tool), give it its own digest, separate from the free prose. A host can then report "routing changed" on its own and ask for re-approval on that, without asking again for every typo fix. Hints left inside descriptions would still need text classification like yours.

Data (CC BY 4.0, `changes.jsonl.gz` + `toolsets.jsonl.gz`): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23512760

AI disclosure: drafted with an AI assistant from our data. The counts were recomputed from the published files, and each candidate was checked against its before and after text.

A separate acceptance case for server-level routing summaries is **mixed-purpose servers**: finding the *right server* must not be confused with selecting an *authorized operation* inside it.

Our first-party Production Desk compatibility probe exposes seven tool declarations in the legacy MCP tool list, ranging from a read-only production diagnosis to creating upload sessions and submitting/updating/deleting a brief. This is an actual observed *tool catalog*, not a test of host routing accuracy or tool execution ([read-only evidence and limits](https://github.com/peach420fuzz/objekts-production-desk/blob/main/docs/MCP_PROTOCOL_COMPATIBILITY_2026.md)).

For a user asking “evaluate whether this video shot is feasible, without sending any files,” a one-sentence summary of “AI/VFX production planning and brief submission” might correctly retrieve the server but leave two additional questions unanswered: **which tool** and **whether the user authorized side effects**. The [MCP 2025-11-25 tools spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools) separates `tools/list` from `tools/call`, recommends human oversight, and treats annotations as untrusted unless the server itself is trusted.

A small host-oriented conformance/evaluation matrix could keep these stages independent:

1. **Candidate-server recall:** with deferred tools, does the bounded server description retrieve the relevant MCP server?
2. **Tool-level precision:** after loading the *actual* `tools/list`, does a read-only intent select a diagnosis tool rather than a submission/upload tool?
3. **Negative routing / capability boundary:** if the user asks to render finished video, does the host avoid inferring that a preflight-only server can generate media just because its summary mentions “video production”?
4. **Authorization:** even when the right server and tool are found, is the side-effecting call still blocked pending the applicable approval? Routing metadata should never be treated as that approval.

This is not a proposal to require a new schema field: a concise positive **and negative** scope in the initial server summary plus host-side testing may be enough. It would distinguish an improvement in semantic discovery from an unintended increase in unsafe calls.

Disclosure: I work on AI/VFX production methodology at **objekts**. No quantitative host-routing result is being claimed here.

body:
A correction to my comment above: 12,422 is the number of changes that edited description text and added or removed no tool, not the number that touched a description. In the same snapshot, 14,164 of the 23,821 changes touched a tool description, and 18,599 touched a tool description or a description inside the input or output schema. So a host that flags every description edit would see a routing change about once per 1,200 to 1,500 flags, not once per thousand. The 12 routing changes and the rest of the comment stand. Both counts come straight from `changes.jsonl.gz`: a change counts when its summary lists a modified tool `description`, or a schema path ending in `description`.

On @peach420fuzz's point 4: agreed. Routing metadata can tell a host which server to look at, never what it may do there. A separate digest for it, as suggested above, lets a host notice when that pointer changes without touching the approval of any call.

Written with an AI assistant.
